payload.question: Which model size fits your workflow best?

choices.label: Small + fast (under 1B params)
choices.explanation: Sub-1B models like Harrier 0.6B are the right fit for autocomplete, embedding, and classification — anything where speed beats depth.

choices.label: Balanced (7B params)
choices.explanation: 7B models like Nemotron-Nano give solid chat + reasoning quality on consumer GPUs without the latency tax of larger models.

choices.label: Deep reasoning (15B+)
choices.explanation: 15B and up unlocks Phi-Hero tier responses — slow but thorough. Reserve for one-shot deep dives, not chat turns.

choices.label: Mixture-of-experts (e.g. Qwen3 30B-A3B)
choices.explanation: MoE keeps active params low (3B per token) while the full weight pool sits in VRAM. Strong quality, fast inference, big VRAM bill.

choices.label: A file path on disk
choices.explanation: Close but not quite — a slot points AT a file path (via symlink), but the slot itself is the assignment, not the path.

choices.label: A logical assignment slot for a model
choices.explanation: Exactly. Slots are hardware-aware logical positions (`chat.brain`, `vision.embedder`, `minion.shared`) that get bound to a downloaded model via Apply.

choices.label: A region of RAM
choices.explanation: Not the RAM itself — a slot is the binding from concept (`chat.brain`) to file (`Nemotron-Nano-9B.gguf`). The engine handles where in RAM it loads.

choices.label: A UI component
choices.explanation: Nope — slots are a kernel concept. The wizard renders TILES that represent slots, but the slot itself is the logical assignment.

payload.question: Which inference engine is right for fast code-gen?

choices.label: Burn (Rust-native)
choices.explanation: Burn shines on the embedder + small-LLM side (Harrier 0.6B) — pure Rust, no FFI tax, great for fast token-by-token loops.

choices.label: llama.cpp via FFI
choices.explanation: Battle-tested for GGUF models 7B and up. The right call for Nemotron / Llama-class chat brains where prebuilt kernels win.

choices.label: Candle (HF Rust)
choices.explanation: Best fit for vision models — SigLIP HD runs through Candle. Great Hugging Face interop without Python.

choices.label: candle-vllm (throughput tier)
choices.explanation: Reserve for batched workloads — multi-request throughput beats single-stream latency. Not the default for interactive chat.

payload.question: Embedding vs inference — which one happens FIRST when you hit Send?

choices.label: Embedding
choices.explanation: Right. The minion (Harrier 0.6B + Burn) embeds your message first so the platform can find relevant past memories before the brain inferences a reply.

choices.label: Inference
choices.explanation: Almost — inference does run, but the minion's embedding pass happens FIRST so the brain sees context-aware prompts.

choices.label: Both at the same time
choices.explanation: Not in V1 — the pipeline is sequential (embed → search → assemble context → infer). Parallel speculative paths land later.

payload.question: Why does DevPulse use multiple databases?

choices.label: Legacy decisions nobody fixed
choices.explanation: No — every store was picked deliberately. Each one is best at its job.

choices.label: Each store is best at its specific job
choices.explanation: Yes. libSQL = SSOT for facts; SurrealDB = persona/graph; DuckDB = analytics OLAP; Qdrant = embedded vector. One DB-of-everything would lose on at least one axis.

choices.label: Compliance / regulation
choices.explanation: Not the driver — picks were performance-driven, not legal-driven.

choices.label: It looks impressive in docs
choices.explanation: Sometimes that's the real answer. Not here — each store earns its place.

payload.question: Your laptop has 8 GB of VRAM. Which tier should the wizard pick?

choices.label: High — load everything
choices.explanation: 8 GB can't host a 15B+ model comfortably. The wizard would pick High only for 16 GB+.

choices.label: Mid — 7B chat brain + 0.6B minion
choices.explanation: Right tier. 7B quantized fits in ~6 GB; 0.6B minion + embedder + KV cache rounds out the budget without thrashing.

choices.label: Low — minion only, CPU brain
choices.explanation: Too conservative. The wizard reserves Low for sub-6 GB GPUs or integrated graphics.

choices.label: CPU mode — skip the GPU
choices.explanation: Only if your GPU is unsupported. With 8 GB of usable VRAM, GPU wins on every workload that fits.

payload.question: Constrained decoding via llguidance — what's its role?

choices.label: Speed up token generation
choices.explanation: Indirect — constraint pruning can speed sampling but the GOAL is correctness, not throughput.

choices.label: Force output to match a grammar
choices.explanation: Yes. llguidance prunes logits at sample time so the next token is valid against a CFG / regex / JSON-schema. Used for RRO + tool-call surfaces.

choices.label: Filter the output after it's generated
choices.explanation: That's post-processing — fragile and wasteful. Constrained decoding works DURING generation; tokens that would violate the grammar never get sampled.

payload.question: Why does Clyffy persona live in SurrealDB namespaces (not a config file)?

choices.label: SurrealDB is faster than a file
choices.explanation: Not the reason — a TOML file would be faster to read. The graph-shape is what matters here.

choices.label: Persona traits + relationships are graph-shaped
choices.explanation: Right. Personas have traits, traits relate to memories, memories relate to past sessions. Graph queries on that shape beat any flat file.

choices.label: SurrealDB encrypts at rest
choices.explanation: Encryption isn't the driver — the encrypted-at-rest layer lives in the OS keyring + libSQL for secrets.
